clue.text: Temporary vintage carrier bag for one girl

parts.note: to bag a prize is to win it, the verb rather than the shopping bag of the surface
'for one' is how a clue says e.g., the abbreviation for 'for example'
a lass is a girl, chiefly in northern English

explanation.walkthrough: Three everyday words, none of them meaning what the sentence about shopping wants them to mean, and no instruction between them beyond laying them end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Temporary vintage carrier -> WINEGLASS: it holds a measure of wine only until you drink it, with 'vintage' standing in for the wine itself.

clue.text: Magnetism reversed like that very strongly repels

indicators.note: reversed tells us the word for magnetism is read from its last letter back to its first

parts.note: magnetism is pull or attraction, a draw
so, as in 'do it so', means in that way
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A physics note: turn magnetism round and it pushes away hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversed' turns DRAW (magnetism, an attraction) into WARD; SO means 'like that' and FF is the musical mark fortissimo.
explanation.definitionFit: To ward off something is to fend it away or keep it at bay, which is what repelling does.

clue.text: Agree offhand about Norway suiting vegans

indicators.note: A thing set about something else has closed round it, so the letter named next is planted inside the word before rather than added on.

parts.note: to nod is to agree without saying anything, and this word opens up to take a letter
N is Norway's international vehicle code, the letter carried on cars registered there
an airy remark is offhand — light, casual and unbothered

explanation.walkthrough: Read as English, 'Agree offhand' is one idea; the clue needs it as two separate words doing separate jobs, which is the seam the surface hides.
explanation.definitionFit: suiting vegans -> NON-DAIRY: made without milk, butter or cream, so it clears the biggest hurdle a vegan diet sets, though not the only one.

clue.text: English cricket side wearing grey refuse to use old bat

indicators.note: What you wear goes on the outside of you, so the word after this is the coat and the letters named before it sit inside it.

parts.note: the plain word, opened up after its first letter to take what the clue puts inside
E is the standard abbreviation for English
a cricket field divides into the off side and the leg side, and the off is the half the batter faces
to boycott something is to refuse to use it, after an Irish land agent his neighbours cut off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old bat' is normally an insult aimed at an elderly woman, and here it means a batsman long retired, which is the whole joke of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: old bat -> GEOFFREY BOYCOTT: England's famously obdurate opening batsman of the 1960s and 70s, so 'bat' means the player and 'old' the retired one.

clue.text: Pest turned up every year then disappeared

indicators.note: In a down entry, up runs back towards the first square, so the two letters named next are written the other way round.

parts.note: something that hid has disappeared from view, and the past tense matches
per annum is Latin for every year and shortens to PA, which climbs the entry here

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as arriving, which is what makes the sentence about an insect work; in the wordplay it is an instruction about direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Pest -> APHID: greenfly and blackfly are aphids, the sap-sucking insects gardeners treat as the classic garden pest, so this defines by example.

clue.text: Bit of music in Psycho arranged for orchestra

indicators.note: Music is arranged by rewriting it for other forces, and letters rearranged the same way land in a fresh order.
A bit of a word is the smallest piece you can break off the front of it, which is its opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letter of music, and the only part of the word wanted
eight more letters of fodder, taken from the film's title along with the word in front of it

explanation.walkthrough: Psycho is italicised because it is Hitchcock's title; those shrieking violins are a fine decoy, since all the clue wants from the film is its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: for orchestra -> SYMPHONIC: written for the full orchestral forces a symphony calls on, so the adjective describes music on that scale.

clue.text: Handle fuse with electric current through it

indicators.note: A current running through something passes inside it, so the letter named goes between the letters of the word beside it.

parts.note: to fuse two pieces of metal is to weld them, and this word splits after its first letter
I is the physicist's symbol for electric current, from the French intensité

explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' is the definition and it is a verb — to handle a sword — not the part you grip, which is what the fusebox picture wants you to think.
explanation.definitionFit: Handle -> WIELD: to wield a tool or a weapon is to handle it with control and purpose, the verb sense rather than the noun.

clue.text: Informally, jam makers turning more to chutney

parts.note: the WI, the Women's Institute, is a British organisation famous for its members' home-made jam

indicators.note: turning means changing shape, so the letters of 'more to chutney' are rearranged

explanation.surface: Jam-making ladies relaxedly switch over to chutney production.
explanation.walkthrough: The WI (Women's Institute) is a British women's organisation famous for jam. 'turning' rearranges MORE TO CHUTNEY into THOUTCEREMONY after WI.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting without ceremony means doing things casually, with no formality, which is what informally means.

clue.text: Obelix irreversibly imbued with magic potion

indicators.note: Something imbued with a substance has it running right through, so the letters wanted are lying inside the words before this.

parts.note: six letters in a row, running out of the end of the name and on into the word beside it

explanation.walkthrough: Obelix fell into the cauldron as a baby in the Asterix books, so the surface is a joke about him and the letters need no more than a careful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: magic potion -> ELIXIR: the alchemists' elixir was the draught that cured every ill or granted long life, which is a magic potion exactly.

clue.text: Pass on joke you hear in summarised version

indicators.note: you hear tells us the answer is something that sounds like those words spoken aloud

parts.note: pass on means die, and a joke is a jest: die jest

explanation.surface: Someone passes a joke along and it gets repeated in shortened form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass on' is not passing something along but dying: DIE plus JEST (joke), and 'you hear' says those words spoken aloud give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A digest is a condensed compilation or summary of longer material, such as a digest of the news.

clue.text: Movement Republican party guards against

indicators.note: A guard stands around whatever it protects, so the letters named either side close over the word that follows.

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for a Republican in American politics
a do is a party — a works do, a birthday do
to lean on something is to lean against it, so the two share that sense

explanation.walkthrough: 'Republican party' reads as one phrase and the clue needs it as two words doing separate jobs, which is the commonest way a surface hides a split.
explanation.definitionFit: Movement -> RONDO: a self-contained movement of a sonata or concerto, the one whose opening tune keeps returning between the episodes.

clue.text: Lame man's right to jog

indicators.note: To jog something is to knock it out of place, and letters knocked out of place settle back in another order.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, exactly the count the enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lame' is doing duty as a verb, and 'right' is not the crossword's usual single letter R here — every one of its letters is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Lame -> HAMSTRING: to hamstring is to cut the tendon behind the knee and cripple, so it means to lame in the literal sense before the figurative one.

clue.text: Mark US agent covered around his neck

parts.note: a scar is the mark an old wound leaves behind
a fed is an FBI or federal agent in American slang

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole phrase at the end, and it means wearing a scarf, not the informal sense of eating something at speed.
explanation.definitionFit: covered around his neck -> SCARFED: wrapped in a scarf, from the verb 'to scarf' meaning to wear one, which is a separate word from scarfing food down.

clue.text: These house torsos with head hidden

indicators.note: with head hidden means the first letter of the word for torsos is taken away

parts.note: torsos are bodies, the trunk without the limbs

explanation.surface: A description of hooded tops covering the upper body, hood up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the garments, which house torsos and hide the head under a hood. 'with head hidden' drops B from BODIES to leave ODIES, after HO.
explanation.definitionFit: 'These' points to the items the rest of the clue describes: hooded tops that cover the torso.

clue.text: Trademark on counterfeit jewel, back-to-front little flowers

indicators.note: In an across clue a piece sitting on another comes after it, so the two letters named first are written second.
A word written back-to-front starts from its final letter, so the thing named beside this is spelled in reverse.

parts.note: a jewel is a STONE, turned round here so that it reads from its last letter
TM is the symbol printed beside a trademarked name
to forge is to counterfeit, and the verb hands over five letters whole

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the tail of the sentence even though it reads as part of it, and the comma after 'jewel' is punctuation the setter may put wherever the surface needs it.
explanation.definitionFit: little flowers -> FORGET-ME-NOTS: the small blue spring flowers of the borage family, named for the plea a lover was supposed to attach to them.

clue.text: Fussy manager runs through ground then home

indicators.note: A letter running through the rest is threaded among them, so it joins the pile being shuffled instead of standing outside it.
Anything ground has been crushed and reassembled, and letters put through that come out in a new order.

parts.note: R is the scorer's abbreviation for runs on a cricket card
eight more letters, which with the one above make the nine the enumeration wants

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a player crossing a pitch and both halves of it are wordplay: a cricketer's single letter, and seven words' worth of nothing but letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fussy manager -> MOTHER HEN: someone who clucks over everyone in their charge, fussing round them the way a hen gathers her chicks.

clue.text: Graduate arranged air-con for penguin

parts.note: an MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate

indicators.note: arranged means put in a new order, so the letters of air-con are shuffled

explanation.surface: A graduate sets up air conditioning to keep a penguin cool.
explanation.walkthrough: MA, a Master of Arts, then 'arranged' reshuffles AIRCON into CARONI after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The macaroni penguin is a crested species of the Southern Ocean, named for its yellow head plumes.

clue.text: Message shortening tenancy brought over

indicators.note: Bringing something over turns it to face the other way, so the letters assembled beside this are read from the end back.

parts.note: marge is British shorthand for margarine, and margarine is a shortening — the fat rubbed into pastry
a let is a tenancy, the flat or room you rent for a term

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortening' looks like an instruction to trim a word and is really a noun for baking fat, which is the whole trap the clue is built on.
explanation.definitionFit: Message -> TELEGRAM: the message wired to a post office and delivered on paper, the standard way to send urgent news before the telephone took over.

clue.text: Old couple going round ruined castle hampered event

indicators.note: going round means the word for couple sits on either side of the remaining letters

parts.note: a brace is a pair, a couple

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters of castle are put in a jumbled order

explanation.surface: An elderly pair circle a castle in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' puts BRACE (couple) around STACLE, the letters of CASTLE that 'ruined' rearranges, making BSTACLERACE, with O for Old in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstacle race is one in which runners are hindered by barriers they must clamber over or under.

clue.text: Roast beef out of this world

parts.note: to beef about something is to carp about it — both are verbs for complaining
ET is Spielberg's extra-terrestrial, and an extra-terrestrial comes from beyond this world

explanation.walkthrough: 'Roast beef' is a Sunday dinner in the surface and two separate jobs in the clue, and reading the pair as one dish is the trap.
explanation.definitionFit: Roast -> CARPET: in British usage to carpet someone is to haul them in for a dressing-down, and to roast them is the same reprimand.

clue.text: Shelter for longer beneath palm tree

indicators.note: In a down entry what lies beneath sits lower in the column, so the piece named before this ends up second.

parts.note: the coco is the coconut palm, the tree itself rather than its fruit
to keep going for longer is to go on, so 'on' carries the sense of continuing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shelter' is a noun here rather than the verb: the case a caterpillar spins round itself, which is why the clue's picture of beach shade is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelter -> COCOON: the silk case a caterpillar spins to protect itself while it pupates, so it is a shelter in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Dull Mondays regularly boring princess

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the picked letters go inside the princess's name

parts.note: Anne is the Princess Royal, the King's sister

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of Mondays, here the second, fourth and sixth

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of Mondays are O, D and Y

explanation.surface: A princess finds Mondays tedious, week in week out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' picks ODY from mOnDaYs, and 'boring' drills them into ANNE, Britain's Princess Royal.
explanation.definitionFit: Anodyne describes something bland and inoffensive, so lacking in interest that it is tedious.

clue.text: End of term decided on by start of last period

definitions.meaning: the surface is a school calendar breaking up for the holidays; the other reading is the end of a pregnancy, which is also called a term

definitions.text: decided on by start of last period
definitions.meaning: a timetable's last period is a lesson, but a midwife counts forty weeks from the first day of the previous monthly cycle

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to take apart here: it is one sentence read twice, once in a school and once in a maternity clinic, and every word changes job between them.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight in an obstetric sense: the expected end of gestation, worked out by counting forward from the last menstrual period.

clue.text: Drinker really after drop

indicators.note: A piece that comes after another is written to its right, so the word named before this ends up second in the answer.

parts.note: a drop in the road, or in prices, is a dip
'so' does the same work as 'really' as an intensifier: it was so cold, it was really cold

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drinker' is doing more than naming someone with a glass in hand; the answer is a clipped, faintly clinical word for one who cannot stop.
explanation.definitionFit: Drinker -> DIPSO: British slang shortened from dipsomaniac, so it names not the social drinker but the compulsive one.

clue.text: Doctor visually very attractive, swanky surgery admits

indicators.note: To admit someone is to let them inside, so the words beside this open up and take the earlier letters in.

parts.note: posh is swanky — showily upmarket
calling someone hot is calling them very good-looking
an op is an operation, the surgery a patient goes in for

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is the verb — to tamper with an image — rather than the person in the surgery, and the whole surface exists to keep you reading it the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor -> PHOTOSHOP: the software's name became a verb for retouching a picture, and doctoring an image is exactly that alteration.

clue.text: Well-to-do urbanite keeps something to sniff

indicators.note: What a person keeps they hold on to inside, so the letters wanted are sitting within the words before this.

parts.note: five letters in a row, running out of the hyphenated phrase and on into the word after it

explanation.walkthrough: An urbanite is only a city dweller, a stiff word chosen for the letters it begins with — that awkwardness is the tell worth learning.
explanation.definitionFit: something to sniff -> ODOUR: a smell considered as the thing the nose picks up, and the word leans towards the unpleasant end of them.

clue.text: Principle superficially true and clear

indicators.note: What is superficial sits on the surface, so only the outside letters at each end of the word beside this are taken.

parts.note: the two outer letters of TRUE, one at each end, with its middle left behind
to clear a sum is to net it — what is left once the deductions are done

explanation.walkthrough: 'True and clear' reads as one description of a principle, which is the misdirection: the two words are doing quite separate mechanical jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Principle -> TENET: a belief held as an article of faith by a person or a group, so it is a principle in the doctrinal sense.

clue.text: Metal zip's inside covered by plastic dummy one

indicators.note: covered by means the central letter is enclosed in the other letters
plastic means pliable, able to be moulded, so the letters of dummy and one are reshaped
's inside, read as 'zip's inside', means the central letter of zip, its heart

parts.note: zip has three letters, and its middle one is I

explanation.surface: A baby's plastic dummy has a zip inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plastic' is the anagram signal for DUMMY ONE, giving NEODYMUM; ''s inside' takes I, the middle of zip, and 'covered by' wraps those reshuffled letters around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Neodymium is a rare-earth metallic element, used in powerful permanent magnets.
